To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) patients with CVID have a higher incidence of autoimmune disorders than the general population, and that this association is more prominent in patients with low IgG levels, (ii) patients with CVD have an increased frequency of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and B cell subsets that are involved in autoantibody production, and (iii) the frequency of Tregs is associated with the presence of autoimmunity in patients with CVID.

the presence of autoimmunity was associated with regulatory T cells in patients with CVID and that the presence of B cell subsets, such as B cells expressing IgM, IgD, CD19, CD21, CD23, CD24, and CD27 was associated with regulatory B cells in patients with common-variable immunodeficiency.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we found that regulatory T cells (Tregs) and B cells are involved in the pathogenesis of common variable immunodeficiencies (CVIDs), and the clinical phenotype of the disease is associated with the level of Treg function.

we have shown that the presence of autoimmunity is a feature of patients with CVID and that the presence of this feature may be associated with a reduction in the number and function of T regulatory cells and an increase in the numbers of B1 cells.
the majority of patients with CVID have autoimmunity and that the presence of regulatory T cell dysfunction is associated with a greater degree of autoimmune manifestations.

we have shown that there is an increased prevalence of autoimmunity in patients with CVID.
we have a better understanding of how B cells contribute to autoimmune disease in the context of CVID.
the B cell repertoire of patients with CVID is not as limited in its diversity as previously thought.
